title: Anatomy, Abdomen and Pelvis: Superior Mesenteric Artery

sections.Introduction:
The superior mesenteric artery (SMA) is the 2nd major branch of the abdominal aorta. Originating from the anterior surface of the aorta at the level of the L1 vertebra, the artery arises approximately 1 cm inferior to the celiac trunk and superior to the renal arteries. Anterior relations include the pylorus of the stomach, the neck of the pancreas, and the splenic vein. Posterior relations include the uncinate process of the pancreas, the inferior portion of the duodenum, and the left renal vein. The left renal vein courses directly between the aorta and the origin of the SMA. The SMA supplies the 3rd portion of the duodenum, jejunum, ileum, cecum, ascending colon, and proximal transverse colon.[1][2][3]

The anatomic relationships and collateral pathways of the SMA underlie several clinically important conditions, including acute mesenteric ischemia, SMA syndrome, and nutcracker syndrome. Recognition of this blood vessel's branching pattern and common sites of occlusion or compression is critical for interpreting imaging studies, planning surgical approaches, performing endovascular interventions, and managing mesenteric vascular emergencies. A thorough understanding of the SMA's anatomy and function enables clinicians to localize pathology, anticipate complications, and optimize diagnostic and therapeutic decision-making across medical and surgical specialties.
sections.Structure and Function:
The SMA supplies the midgut from the ampullary region of the 2nd part of the duodenum to the splenic flexure of the large intestine (see Image. Superior Mesenteric Artery). The inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery arises from the SMA and, together with the superior pancreaticoduodenal artery, supplies the head of the pancreas.

Marginal Artery of Drummond

The distal SMA branches, including the right colic, ileocolic, and middle colic arteries, supply the colon. The inferior mesenteric artery (IMA) perfuses the colon through the sigmoid and left colic arteries. An intricate arterial arcade along the mesenteric border, known as the marginal artery of Drummond, connects these branches. The marginal artery of Drummond is a normal vascular structure in many healthy individuals but may be absent in others. The marginal artery of Drummond is clinically significant because it provides collateral circulation to the colon when mesenteric vessels become occluded. Absence of this vascular structure increases the risk of bowel infarction and necrosis following mesenteric ischemia.
sections.Blood Supply and Lymphatics:
The 1st branch of the SMA is the inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery, which bifurcates into anterior and posterior branches that form anastomoses with branches of the superior pancreaticoduodenal artery, a branch of the celiac artery. The inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery supplies the head of the pancreas and the duodenum.

The SMA gives off several jejunal and ileal arteries to the left and the middle colic, right colic, and ileocolic arteries to the right. The jejunal and ileal arteries form anastomotic arcades within the mesentery, giving rise to small, straight end arteries called "vasa recta" that supply the intestinal wall. The jejunal blood supply consists of fewer arterial arcades with numerous long vasa recta. The ileal blood supply contains more arterial arcades with fewer, shorter vasa recta.

The middle colic artery supplies the transverse colon, while the right colic artery supplies the ascending colon. The ileocolic artery is the inferior-most branch of the SMA and supplies the ascending colon, appendix, cecum, and ileum.

The major anastomosis between the SMA and IMA is the marginal artery of Drummond, which supplies the splenic flexure. A more proximal anastomosis between the SMA and IMA is formed by the Arc of Riolan, also known as the meandering artery. The Arc of Riolan is typically an arterial anastomosis between the middle colic artery, a branch of the SMA, and the left colic artery, a branch of the IMA.[4]
sections.Surgical Considerations:
SMA stenosis or occlusion can lead to acute mesenteric ischemia. Delayed recognition can result in bowel gangrene. Reduced SMA flow may occur secondary to hypotension from any cause, whereas SMA occlusion may result from atherosclerosis or embolism.[5][6][7][8]

Most acute mesenteric arterial emboli originate from cardiac sources. Classic causes include atrial thrombi, mural thrombi following myocardial infarction, atrial fibrillation, mycotic aneurysms, and thrombi from atherosclerotic plaques.

SMA arterial thrombosis is usually due to visceral atherosclerosis. Symptoms typically do not appear until extensive occlusion of the mesenteric arterial branches occurs. Progressive thrombus formation causes gradual reduction in blood flow, eventually resulting in postprandial abdominal pain. Delayed recognition can lead to bowel necrosis. Elevated serum lactate levels may occur with bowel ischemia. Emergent computed tomography (CT) angiography of the abdomen is indicated when acute mesenteric ischemia is suspected.[9]

Treatment options for acute SMA thrombosis include open surgery, percutaneous angioplasty with stenting, and thrombolytic therapy. Delayed treatment is associated with very high mortality.[10][11]

Nonocclusive mesenteric ischemia results from decreased bowel perfusion. Causes include septic shock, myocardial infarction, hypovolemia, and high-dose vasopressor use, which can induce vasoconstriction.
sections.Clinical Significance:
The marginal artery, also known as the artery of Drummond, supplies the proximal descending colon at the splenic flexure. The artery of Drummond is an arterial arcade formed by an anastomosis between the distal branches of the SMA and IMA. The anastomosis is often weak and tortuous and may be absent. Therefore, the splenic flexure is a watershed area prone to ischemia and infarction in the setting of hypoperfusion.

Sudden SMA occlusion causes acute mesenteric ischemia. The condition is a surgical emergency associated with high mortality.

Nutcracker syndrome results from compression of the left renal vein between the SMA and abdominal aorta. Manifestations may include hematuria, abdominal pain, and left testicular pain in men or left lower quadrant pain in women. Symptoms result from left gonadal vein outflow obstruction, as the left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein.[12]

SMA syndrome occurs when the 3rd and 4th portions of the duodenum become compressed between the abdominal aorta and the SMA. Symptoms include early satiety, nausea, vomiting, and sharp postprandial abdominal pain due to small bowel obstruction.[13]
